column5: Grollemund et al. 2015 (PNAS, 424 languages): the Bantu in-group dates to about 4,800 years ago (4,846 plus or minus 138), the homeland is in north-western Cameroon savannah, the main route went south-east then east along the southern edge of the rainforest following savannah corridors (Sangha River Interval, from about 2,500 years ago), not a coastal or rainforest route, and the Eastern Bantu of the Great Lakes descend from the main backbone, not from a northern Congo migration. Course says several waves and routes and 'disputes about the main route': add that this paper favours one backbone along savannah corridors, a model result, [PROBABLE].

Paper: movement from savannah into rainforest took about 300 years longer than comparable savannah moves (662.8 plus or minus 78.7 against 368.6 years, a pace cut of about 50 per cent), citing Vansina that farmers took about 2,000 years to settle the equatorial forest. Adds a quantified, model-based rate to Module 1 lesson 3; the dates depend on four archaeological calibration points and the 100-word lists for 424 languages, so tag [PROBABLE] and say it is a model.

Supplement: dates are anchored on Shum Laka (Ceramic Late Stone Age, about 5,000 to 4,000 years ago, in Cameroon's Grassfields), Obobogo near Yaounde (earliest village, about 3,500 to 3,000 years ago) and the Urewe tradition (about 2,500 years ago, Eastern Bantu). Useful for Module 1: the linguistic tree is tied to archaeology, so it is a model calibrated on three sites, not an independent count. Note: chunk 3 (the reference list) was served without my reading it line by line.
